e.t: This Hebrew word means “love.” It names love as a reality expressed in relationships, including love involving God and people. The surrounding passage determines the specific expression, but the word’s consistent central sense is love.

This Hebrew word refers to the Geshurites, a people associated with the region of Geshur. It functions as a people-name rather than as a general description or action. The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy, Joshua, and 1 Samuel. Its references consistently identify the Geshurites as a distinct population among the peoples and territories mentioned in Israel’s history. The exact significance in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “trouble,” expressing an action that brings trouble upon someone or something. It is found three times in the Old Testament, all in two verses in Ezekiel 32. It means “clean,” describing a person or condition regarded as clean. This Hebrew word functions as a predicate: it tells what someone or something is considered to be. It appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Micah. Its precise force depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains being clean rather than defiled.

“Sweat” refers to moisture produced by the body, especially through exertion or heat. This Hebrew noun names something physical rather than expressing an action or command. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 3:19. The word identifies a bodily substance, while its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its meaning is therefore concrete and straightforward: sweat.

This Hebrew verb means “hide”: to conceal oneself or something from view or discovery. It describes the act of taking cover or keeping something out of sight, rather than merely being unseen. e.h: A Hebrew Word for the Speaker
e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the person who is speaking—the speaker himself or herself. It is a first-person self-reference, used when someone identifies, describes, or speaks about their own actions and responsibilities. The word appears 359 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi, showing that it is a common way for a speaker to point to himself or herself. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding statement and who is speaking.

Its exact sense depends on how it functions in the surrounding sentence. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Judges, and Kings. Scripture therefore presents it across both an action and a divination-related use, rather than as a single uniform English word.

Athaiah is a personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Because no explicit definition is preserved here, the safest understanding is simply the individual’s name as rendered “Athaiah.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and cannot be established from the name alone.

Its normal sense is straightforward: it identifies darkness itself rather than an action or person. The surrounding verse determines whether the darkness is being described physically or in another setting.

This Hebrew word means “locks,” naming the locks referred to in the Hebrew Old Testament. It occurs four times, in four verses: three times in Song of Songs and once in Isaiah. Its repeated rendering as “locks” supports a concrete meaning rather than an abstract idea. The word therefore identifies a visible feature, while the surrounding verse determines whose locks are being described and what is being said about them.

The word occurs four times in the Old Testament, appearing in Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains clear and consistent across these occurrences.

This Hebrew word means “madness,” describing a state or expression of severely disordered thinking or behavior. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the inward state or the outward behavior, but its central idea remains madness rather than ordinary distress or confusion.

e.t: Samuel is a personal name, referring to the man Samuel in the Hebrew Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than as a description, command, or general idea. The name appears 140 times in the Hebrew corpus, with most occurrences in 1 Samuel, and it is also used in references extending from Numbers through Jeremiah. Scripture presents the name in settings involving Samuel’s speech, service, leadership, and relationship to God’s people, but the word itself identifies the person rather than expressing those activities. English renderings consistently give it as “Samuel.”

e.t: “Sherebiah” is a Hebrew personal name identifying a particular man, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears eight times in the Old Testament, especially in Ezra and Nehemiah. The name is associated with the community’s leaders and Levites during the return from exile, the teaching of the Law, public prayer, and worship. Because it functions as a name, its ordinary role is to identify the person called Sherebiah; the surrounding passage is needed to explain what he is doing in any particular verse.

It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Samuel 6:19 and once in 1 Chronicles 16:3. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the word’s precise force in each passage cannot be explained further; its established lexical sense remains the simple description “good.”

e.t: Sheshan is a personal name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs five times, all within three verses in 1 Chronicles 2, where the surrounding patterns place the name within genealogical material and connect it with giving and birth or begetting. Thus, readers should understand “Sheshan” as the individual’s name; its precise role in each genealogical statement depends on the verse context.

This Hebrew word means “went,” expressing the act of moving from one place or position to another. It functions as a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:31. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly who went and how the action fits that passage; the word itself centers on the action of going.

This Hebrew word means “perfection.” It functions as a noun, naming perfection as a quality or state rather than describing an action. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, at Psalm 119:96, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses. The word is connected there with a statement involving God’s commandment, but the verse’s precise force requires the surrounding text. Its recorded English rendering is consistently “perfection.”

This Hebrew verb means “sewed,” describing the act of sewing. It appears four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, each time in a different verse. Its use covers ordinary action as well as figurative or poetic descriptions, but the basic idea remains the same: sewing. The surrounding passage determines what is being sewn and why, while the word itself identifies the action. It is found from Genesis through Ezekiel, showing continued use across different Old Testament books.
